headline: High: shared filesystem and broad egress create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-action risks between Continue and kotaemon.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Continue can read/write workspace files and use MCP, while kotaemon processes documents, PDFs, HTML, and chat transcripts. Their shared filesystem path makes attacker-controlled content from one agent plausibly consumed by the other as instructions. This is not proven by direct interaction evidence, so I choose medium over low because the pathway exists in default-ish setups.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace or document store, injected instructions can cross from one to the other.
IF kotaemon ingests a file produced by Continue without provenance filtering, prompt text can be treated as instructions.
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent.
Disable MCP servers that are not required.
Add provenance labels to files before handoff.
Review any file-based handoff before opening it in the other agent.
requires-engineering: enforce content-sanitization or instruction-stripping at the bridge.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Continue touches source code, open editor buffers, and model-provider API keys; kotaemon touches documents, PDFs, chat transcripts, and API keys, and both have broad network egress. If they share files or credentials, sensitive content can flow from one agent into the other's outbound API calls. The pairwise leakage path is plausible from the profiles, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF both agents can access the same files, documents or editor buffers may be uploaded by either backend.
IF the same API key or OAuth principal is reused, one agent's sensitive context can be exposed through the other's requests.
mitigations: Use separate API keys per agent.
Restrict each agent to distinct directories.
Remove secrets from shared workspaces.
Turn off network egress for the less-trusted agent when possible.
requires-engineering: add per-agent access controls and audit logging.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Continue can write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses; kotaemon writes to ./ktem_app_data and can use Docker plus multiple instances. They therefore overlap on mutable local state and can race on shared files if co-located. I do not see git locking or other coordination, so the conflict is real but not clearly high.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same directory tree, they can overwrite each other's files.
IF kotaemon instances share ./ktem_app_data, concurrent writes can corrupt state.
mitigations: Assign separate working directories.
Avoid running multiple instances against the same data folder.
Back up shared state before concurrent use.
Pause one agent while the other writes.
requires-engineering: add file locks or transactional writes.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Continue can generate code or file edits, and kotaemon is a RAG/chat system that can consume documents and citations. If kotaemon treats Continue's output as authoritative, errors can cascade into downstream answers or actions. There is no explicit verification layer in either profile, so the interaction is plausible and merits medium severity.
conditions: IF kotaemon ingests Continue-generated text without verification, hallucinations can be amplified.
IF Continue writes summaries that kotaemon later cites, incorrect facts can propagate into user-facing outputs.
mitigations: Require human review before reuse of generated text.
Mark machine-generated files clearly.
Cross-check citations against source documents.
Limit kotaemon to source-grounded retrieval only.
requires-engineering: add provenance-aware verification between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: Continue is an IDE assistant handling source code and editor buffers, while kotaemon handles documents, chat transcripts, and API keys with broad network egress. The profiles do not specify residency or certifications, so I cannot prove a breach, but the mixed data classes and outbound APIs create a plausible retention and disclosure mismatch. Uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF regulated documents or secrets are placed into kotaemon, they may be retained or transmitted under different policies than Continue.
IF the two agents are used under different data-handling obligations, shared content can violate the stricter policy.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared workflows.
Use separate retention settings where available.
Document which data classes each agent may process.
Review outbound API destinations before use.
requires-engineering: align residency, retention, and deletion controls across both tools.
